> **Session focus:** *Role in collaborations, Code of Conduct, collaboration tips, mentorship, and communicating statistics to clinicians*

## Learning Objectives

* Clarify the professional identity of biostatisticians in collaborations
* Apply the Biostatistician’s Code of Conduct to realistic scenarios
* Communicate statistical ideas clearly to clinicians and avoid common language pitfalls
* Distinguish statistical significance from clinical relevance in decision-making

## Description of Activities

On 14 April (Block 2), the day covered our role in collaborations, the Biostatistician’s Code of Conduct, practical tips for enhancing collaborations, and mentorship in academia. Complementary sessions focused on communicating statistics to clinicians, avoiding misuse of statistical language and methods, and contrasting statistical significance with clinical relevance in interventional research.

## Reflection (Gibbs Reflective Cycle)

### 1. Description

Today I stopped seeing myself only as a data analyst. I left with a clearer picture of my role: collaborate, teach, and act with integrity. We covered the Code of Conduct, practical habits that make collaborations work, how to speak with clinicians about statistics, and why clinical relevance matters beyond p‑values. Together, the sessions framed collaboration as ethical work that depends on clear communication.

### 2. Feelings

I felt energized by the expanded view of my role and aware of the responsibility my advice carries. The communication session made “clarity” feel learnable and practical. Mentorship was motivating, with some nerves about starting those relationships well.

### 3. Evaluation

The pieces fit together: ethics set the guardrails; tips turned principles into behaviors; communication improved precision; mentorship made growth feel doable. We had less time for the grey areas, like balancing time pressure with rigor.

### 4. Analysis

A simple checklist helps me show up well: bring the right attitude, set structure early (scope, expectations, authorship), co‑create questions, communicate plainly, and invest in trust over time. I noticed a bias to define my value as “technical.” Today expanded that to “partner” who helps turn numbers into decisions.

### 5. Conclusion

Effective collaboration blends ethics, relationships, and translation. Accuracy matters, but impact depends on making results usable to clinicians.

### 6. Action Plan

I will keep a conduct checklist (conflicts, authorship, reproducibility), open meetings with a short agenda, and maintain a terminology watchlist to avoid common misuse. I’ll identify mentors whom I can call on with with clear questions to discuss my assumptions and the clinical relevance of my advice.
